SUBJECT:  RECEIVE AND FILE THE MONTHLY INVESTMENT ACTIVITY
  REPORTS FOR FEBRUARY 2026

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Receive and file the February 2026 monthly investment activity reports for the
  City of Palmdale and Successor Agency.

BACKGROUND

In accordance with Section 16 of the City and Successor Agency Investment Policy, the
City Treasurer is required to prepare and present monthly and quarterly investment
reports to the City Manager/Executive Director and the City Council/Board of Directors.
These reports include detailed information on each investment, including the investment
type, issuer name, purchase date, maturity date, amount invested, and interest rate.
Reporting covers all pooled investments of the City and Successor Agency, as well as
Certificates of Participation, Revenue Bonds, Tax Allocation Bonds, Assessment
Districts, and Community Facilities District accounts managed by external fiscal agents.

The monthly investment reports provide an overview of the City and Successor Agency’s
investment activity and portfolio performance. They summarize total assets, portfolio
allocations, average maturities, yields, and book values. The interest rates presented
reflect the most current rates available as of the report date.

Market values for pooled City and Successor Agency investments are based on closing
prices as of the report date. Pricing information is obtained from reputable sources,
including the Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg Financial Markets, Capital Market Finance
publications, and other reliable market data providers.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Monthly Investment Reports February 2026
April 7, 2026
Page 2

DISCUSSION

Compliance with Investment Policy

As of February, the City’s total investment portfolio was valued at $310,283,163,
reflecting a decrease of $324,631 from the prior month and a decrease of $9,380,488
compared to the same period last year. The month-over-month decrease is attributable
to maturities that have not been reinvested yet.

The Successor Agency’s portfolio had a par value of $15,531,671 as of February,
representing a decrease of $1,743,608 from the previous month. The decrease is due
to the debt service payments made during the month.

All investments are in full compliance with Section 8 of the City’s Investment Policy. The
portfolios consist of a diversified mix of authorized investment instruments, including
Certificates of Deposit, Corporate Notes, U.S. Treasury Securities, and Government
Agency Securities, each maintained within established portfolio percentage limits.

The Finance Division serves as custodian of the City and Successor Agency investment
portfolios and adheres to the three primary objectives outlined in the Investment Policy:

    Safeguard principal by investing in financial instruments that mitigate the risk of
  market-related losses;

    Maintain sufficient liquidity to meet anticipated cash flow needs; and

    Achieve a competitive market rate of return consistent with policy constraints.

Liquidity

Maintaining adequate liquidity to support operational requirements remains a key priority
of the Finance Division. To support this objective, the City and Successor Agency invest
in two pooled funds: the Local Agency Investment Fund (LAIF) and the California Asset
Management Program (CAMP). These funds are designed to support daily operational
needs and provide flexibility during periods of economic uncertainty. Their high liquidity
ensures that both entities can meet ongoing cash flow demands.

At the end of February, the City’s LAIF balance totaled $116,929,296, no changes from
the prior month. The Successor Agency’s LAIF balance was $4,027,756, reflecting no
changes from the prior month.

The City’s CAMP balance at the end of February was $54,427,027, compared to
$54,267,675 in January. The increase is due to interest earned during the month.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Monthly Investment Reports February 2026
April 7, 2026
Page 3

The interest rates presented reflect the most current rates available as of the date of this
report. As of February 28, 2026, LAIF and CAMP were earning 3.871 percent and 3.83
percent, respectively. At the end of January, the rates were 3.931 percent for LAIF and
3.85 percent for CAMP. One year ago, LAIF and CAMP rates were 4.333 percent and
4.51 percent, respectively.

The chart above shows the LAIF and CAMP average monthly yields from May 2025
through February 2026. The difference between the two funds’ performance is primarily
due to their varying pool characteristics. CAMP’s portfolio composition is more prone to
market volatility, resulting in performance variations.

Diversity

The Finance Division seeks to maintain a well-diversified investment portfolio in order
to minimize exposure to risks associated with any single security type or financial
institution.

The City and Successor Agency portfolios remain appropriately diversified in
accordance with the Investment Policy. The accompanying monthly reports detail all
investments held by both entities, including current book values as of February 28, 2026.

Based on current projections, both the City and the Successor Agency have sufficient
funds to meet anticipated expenditure requirements over the next six months. The
Finance Division will continue to closely monitor economic conditions and assess their
potential impact on interest rates and overall portfolio performance.

SUBJECT:  APPROVE AGREEMENT WITH DELL INC., FOR MICROSOFT
  AZURE CLOUD SERVICES FOR A THREE-YEAR TERM

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve Agreement No. A-9808 with Dell Inc., for Microsoft Azure cloud services
  for a three-year term; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager or his designee to execute Agreement No. A-9808
  with Dell Inc., including minimal and/or non-substantial changes.

BACKGROUND

The City utilizes Microsoft Azure cloud services to support its core technology
infrastructure, including virtual servers, data storage, and network resources necessary
for daily operations. These services are currently accessed through a Microsoft
Enterprise Agreement (EA), which is scheduled to expire on April 30, 2026.

Cloud-based infrastructure has replaced traditional on-premises systems as the
standard for public agencies, allowing organizations to avoid large capital investments
in physical hardware while maintaining reliable and secure access to systems and data.
Continuation of these services is necessary to ensure uninterrupted access to the City’s
applications and operational systems.

DISCUSSION

Approval of Agreement No. A-9808 will allow the City to continue utilizing Microsoft
Azure cloud services that support essential municipal operations. These services
provide the computing environment required to host applications, manage data, and
maintain system availability.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Approve Agrmt. No. A-9808 with Dell Inc.
April 7, 2026
Page 2

Microsoft Azure operates under a consumption-based pricing model, where costs are
based on actual service usage rather than a fixed contract amount. Because resource
needs vary over time due to operational demands, system changes, and technology
initiatives, total costs cannot be predetermined. Microsoft structures these agreements
without not-to-exceed amounts, as charges are directly tied to real-time usage.

The Agreement was procured through a cooperative purchasing program, ensuring that
pricing is competitively established and consistent with rates available to other public
agencies. This approach allows the City to efficiently obtain services while maintaining
cost competitiveness.

The proposed Agreement will establish a new three-year term with Dell Inc., an
authorized reseller, allowing the City to maintain continuity of services through April
2029.

FISCAL IMPACT

Estimated to range from $234,000 to $288,000; Costs are dependent on service
consumption and may vary. It is anticipated that monthly charges will range between
$6,500 and $8,000, which totals an estimated cost of $234,000 to $288,000 over the
three-year term. Funds are budgeted and available in Information Technology accounts
for FY 2025-26. Subsequent years will be proposed through the annual budget process.

STRATEGIC PLAN

Goal III: Ensure long-term fiscal health of the city and maintain funding for services.

  A. Manage resources, costs, and liabilities to ensure the City’s long-term fiscal
  health.

SUBJECT:  APPROVE THE CERTIFICATE OF COMPLETION BETWEEN THE
  CITY OF PALMDALE AND DELTA SCIENTIFIC CORPORATION AS
  REQUIRED BY AGREEMENT NO. A-0155 FOR THE DEVELOPMENT
  OF TWO INDUSTRIAL BUILDINGS LOCATED ON THE
  SOUTHWEST CORNER OF AVENUE O AND DELTA LANE (APN’S
  3005-046-016 AND -017)

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve the Certificate of Completion between the City of Palmdale and Delta
  Scientific Corporation as required by Agreement No. A-0155 for the development
  of two industrial buildings located on the southwest corner of Avenue O and Delta
  Lane (APN’s 3005-046-016 and -017); and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager or his designee to execute the Certificate of
  Completion with Delta Scientific Corporation, including minimal and/or non-
  substantive changes.

BACKGROUND

The project site consists of two parcels totaling 8.72 acres located on the southwest
corner of Avenue O and Delta Lane within the Fairway Business Park. The northerly
5.89 acres is owned by Delta Scientific (Delta) and contains an existing 127,850 square
foot industrial building (APN 3005-046-016, 40355 Delta Lane), and the southerly 2.83
acres is owned by Woodleigh Properties (Woodleigh) and contains an existing 59,586
square foot industrial building (APN 3005-046-017, 305 Grand Cypress Avenue).

Delta Scientific agreed to develop the property under a Disposition and Development
Agreement (DDA) dated December 11, 2002 (recorded December 19, 2002, as
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Certificate of Completion
April 7, 2026
Page 2

Instrument No. 02-3125449) and later acquired the property from the City by Grant Deed
dated April 14, 2003 (recorded May 28, 2003, as Instrument No. 03-1505617).

DISCUSSION

Delta and Woodleigh are currently in the process of selling the site and have requested
that the City clarify and confirm certain matters related to the DDA and the Grant Deed.
Development of the site was completed in 2004 for the northerly parcel and in 2006 for
the southerly parcel. Under the DDA, the City is required to issue and record a Certificate
of Completion confirming satisfactory completion of the development upon request by
Delta and Woodleigh. Although the Certificate should have been recorded when the
project was completed approximately twenty years ago, Delta and Woodleigh have
recently requested that the City issue the attached Certificate.

The Grant Deed restricts transfer of the parcels for a period of ten years following
recordation of the Certificate of Completion. Because the Certificate of Completion will
be recorded now (if approved by City Council), applying this provision as written would
effectively impose a new ten-year restriction on the property owners’ ability to sell the
parcels (through 2036), which does not reflect the original intent of the DDA or the Grant
Deed.

Staff has determined that the site was developed in accordance with the terms and
conditions of the DDA and therefore is recommending that the City Council formally
acknowledge satisfactory completion of the project and termination of the restriction on
transfer tied to the date of recordation of the Certificate of Completion. The attached
Certificate of Completion acknowledges the following:

    There are no breaches or defaults under the Grant Deed, and all construction
  and development obligations for the site have been fully satisfied.
    The City confirms that all obligations of Delta under the Grant Deed have been
  fully performed in compliance with the DDA, Grant Deed, and the Redevelopment
  Plan and CC&Rs for the Fairway Business Park.
    Any restrictions on the sale, transfer, assignment, or leasing of the site are
  terminated and the site may be freely transferred.
    The City has no right to reenter, take possession of, or reclaim the site.
    The City has no right of first refusal, no right of reverter, and no other reversionary
  interest in the site.

  EXEMPTION AND AUTHORIZING A MULTI-YEAR CITYWIDE
  RIGHT-OF-WAY  MAINTENANCE  AND  REHABILITATION
  PROGRAM FROM FISCAL YEAR 2025-26 TO FISCAL YEAR 2030-
  31

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2026-005, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
  Palmdale affirming CEQA exemption and authorizing a multi-year citywide right-
  of-way maintenance and rehabilitation program from Fiscal Year 2025-26 and
  Fiscal Year 2030-31;

  2. Approve implementation of ongoing Citywide Maintenance and Rehabilitation
  Program;

  3. Authorize Citywide Annual Pavement Management Program (CAPM) projects
  consistent with the approved program and exemption; and,

  4. Direct staff to file a Notice of Exemption (NOE) with the Los Angeles County
  Clerk.

BACKGROUND

The City maintains an extensive network of public streets, sidewalks, curbs, gutters,
driveways, and traffic control devices. To preserve public safety, comply with ADA
requirements, and protect prior infrastructure investments, the City proposes to continue
an ongoing Citywide Annual Pavement Maintenance and Rehabilitation Program
(CAPM). CAPM consists exclusively of repair, maintenance, replacement, and
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Adopt Reso. No. CC 2026-005
April 7, 2026
Page 2

reconstruction of existing facilities within existing public right-of-way and does not
involve roadway widening, capacity expansion, or land use changes. As such, the
program poses no significant impacts and qualifies for a categorical exemption from
CEQA. Adoption of this item establishes a programmatic CEQA determination, allowing
staff to implement annual CAPM projects while maintaining full CEQA compliance.

DISSCUSION

The City annually implements pavement rehabilitation, including sidewalk repair, ADA
curb ramp upgrades, curb and gutter replacement, and traffic sign and striping
improvements, as part of its CAPM for broader public works maintenance efforts.
Historically, these projects have been delivered as separate construction activities;
however, they are fundamentally part of a continuous maintenance program addressing
systemwide infrastructure needs. Establishing a program-level CEQA exemption
provides clarity, efficiency, and legal defensibility.

The Program qualifies for a categorical exemption under CEQA Guidelines Sections:

  •  15301(a) and (c) – Existing Facilities; and,
  •  15302 – Replacement or Reconstruction.

Involves no expansion of roadways, no increased roadway capacity, and no change in
land use. All activities occur within the existing public right-of-way. No exceptions under
CEQA Guidelines, Section 15300.2 apply.

The CAMP includes, but is not limited to:

    Asphalt concrete overlays, slurry seal, cape seal, grinding, full deck replacement,
  and localized pavement repairs;
    Repair and replacement of sidewalks, driveway aprons, curbs, gutters, and curb
  ramps;
    ADA accessibility upgrades to existing pedestrian facilities;
    Replacement and installation of regulatory traffic signs, pavement markings, and
  striping; and,
    Minor excavation, backfill, and surface restoration.

All work is limited to existing, previously disturbed public right-of-way and maintains the
same purpose and capacity of existing facilities. Staff will perform annual CEQA
consistency determinations to confirm continued eligibility.

Projects are implemented in accordance with the City’s Complete Streets policies and the
Americans with Disabilities Act. Improvements include pedestrian safety enhancements,
curb ramp upgrades, and sidewalk repairs without adding vehicular capacity.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Adopt Reso. No. CC 2026-005
April 7, 2026
Page 3

Project prioritization incorporates CalEnviroScreen and the LA Metro Equity Platform
to identify and prioritize investments in disadvantaged and underserved communities with
documented environmental, health, and access needs. This data-driven approach directs
funding toward projects that improve safety, mobility, and accessibility for vulnerable
populations while remaining limited to planning, safety, and minor infrastructure actions
that do not result in a significant environmental impact. Accordingly, use of these equity
and screening tools supports transparent, needs-based decision-making and does not
affect the project’s eligibility for exemption under CEQA.

FISCAL IMPACT

$0; There is no fiscal impact associated with this action; however, funding for projects will
be provided through a combination of Measure R, Measure M, SB-1, Gas Tax, and/or
other eligible transportation funds, subject to annual capital budget appropriation. This
Resolution will clear the entire right-of-way, making all resurfacing, reconstruction, and
replacement of all right-of-way assets shovel-ready as defined by the Los Angeles
Metropolitan Transportation Agency and Caltrans.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2026-006, a Resolution of the City Council of the City
  of Palmdale, directing the preparation of the annual Engineer’s Report for the
  continuation of the annual levy of assessments and designating the Engineer of
  Work for the City of Palmdale Drainage Benefit Assessment Districts No. 1, and
  No. 2006-02; and,

  2. Authorize the Mayor to execute Resolution No. CC 2026-006, directing the
  preparation of the annual Engineer’s Report for the continuation of the annual
  levy of assessments and designating the Engineer of Work for the City of
  Palmdale Drainage Benefit Assessment Districts No. 1, and No. 2006-02.

BACKGROUND

During the entitlement review of the Anaverde and Ritter Ranch developments, it was
determined that the formation of drainage benefit assessment districts was necessary
to fund the maintenance of drainage facilities for each of these Master Planned
Communities. As a result, the formation of the Drainage Benefit Assessment Districts
No. 1 (Anaverde), and No. 2006-02 (Ritter Ranch) were approved by the property
owners on May 12, 2004, and January 3, 2007, respectively, pursuant to mailed ballot
elections conducted in accordance with Article XIIID of the California Constitution.
 Report to Mayor and City Council

April 7, 2026

The purpose of the Drainage Benefit Assessment Districts is to fund the installation,
construction, and/or maintenance of any authorized improvements under the Benefit
Assessment Act of 1982 (California Government Code Section 54703 et seq.). These
improvements include, but are not limited to, drainage improvements and any facilities
appurtenant to those improvements, or necessary or convenient for their maintenance
and servicing.

DISCUSSION

Resolution No. CC 2026-006 designates NBS as the Engineer of Work and directs the
preparation of the annual Engineer’s Report for Fiscal Year 2026-27 for the City of
Palmdale Drainage Benefit Assessment Districts No. 1, and No. 2006-02.

Each year, in order for the City to continue to levy annual assessments within the
Drainage Benefit Assessment Districts, the City must have a detailed Engineer’s Report
approved by the City Council. The attached resolution, ordering the preparation of the
combined annual Engineer’s Report, initiates the proceedings for the annual levy of
assessments for the Drainage Benefit Assessment Districts No. 1, and No. 2006-02 for
Fiscal Year 2026-27.

The annual Engineer’s Report will be presented to the City Council at the June 2, 2026
meeting. A public hearing will be held at the July 7, 2026 City Council meeting in order
to accept public testimony regarding the annual report and authorize the levy of
assessments for Fiscal Year 2026-27.

FISCAL IMPACT

$0; Ther is no fiscal impact associated with this action. Levy amounts will be included
with the Engineer’s Report that will be presented at the June 2, 2026, City Council
meeting.

BACKGROUND

The City’s Landscape Maintenance Assessment Districts and Annexations, Park
Maintenance and Recreation Improvement District, and Streetlight Maintenance
Assessment Districts and Annexations (all together referred to as the “Districts”), were
approved by property owners pursuant to mailed ballot elections conducted in
accordance with Article XIIID of the California Constitution and the Landscaping and
Lighting Act of 1972 (the "Act"), Part 2 of Division 15 of the California Streets and
Highways Code (commencing with Section 22500 thereof).

The purpose of the Landscape Maintenance Assessment Districts and Annexations is
to fund the installation, maintenance, and servicing of ornamental structures,
landscaping, including trees, shrubs, grass, and other ornamental vegetation, and
appurtenant facilities, including irrigation systems, drainage devices, and drywells
located in public places within the boundaries of the Landscape Maintenance

DISCUSSION

The proposed Second Amendment to the Agreement would revise the project scope
and increase the contract amount to address newly identified drainage deficiencies.

A focused sub-drainage hydrological analysis has determined that the original Master
Drainage Plan did not include sufficient data to support the design of effective catch
basins for surface flow containment. Subsequent stormwater analysis indicates that
the existing infrastructure is inadequate to manage current street runoff conditions,
resulting in the need for additional drainage improvements.

To address these deficiencies, the drainage plans will be updated to include four new
catch basins along the east side of 45th Street. Each basin will require site-specific
design to accommodate existing utilities and to ensure proper connection to the
proposed box culvert system.

The additional design work and expanded scope necessitate an increase in the
contract amount of $54,625, for a revised total project cost of $362,365.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve Agreement No. A-9785 with Willdan Engineering for Construction
  Management and Observation Services for PN 796, 45th Street East Sewer, Storm
  Drain and Street Improvement Project (Project), for a total not to exceed amount
  of $877,189, which includes a contract amount of $762,772, plus a 15%
  contingency amount of $114,417 for a term of 251 working days from the date of
  the Notice to Proceed;

  2. Authorize the City Manager or his designee to execute Agreement No. A-9785
  with Willdan Engineering, including minimal and/or non-substantial changes; and,

  3. Authorize the City Manager or his designee to approve change orders for
  additional or changed scopes of work up to the 15% contingency amount approved
  by the Council.

BACKGROUND

The Project is a pivotal undertaking to enhance infrastructure along 45th Street between
Avenue R and Avenue S. This initiative aims to improve roadway safety and functionality
while effectively managing stormwater and wastewater in our community.

The Project includes:

    Street Pavement Rehab: Includes new sidewalks, curbs, and gutters for safer

and observation services was publicly advertised via the PlanetBids electronic platform.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve Agreement No. A-9790 with Greenfield Landscaping and Maintenance,
  Inc., for turf removal and replacement services at Marie Kerr Park south soccer
  field for a total not to exceed amount of $154,880, which includes a contract
  amount of $140,800, plus a 10% contingency amount of $14,080 for a term of six
  months; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager or his designee to execute Agreement No. A-9790
  with Greenfield Landscaping and Maintenance, Inc., including minimal and/or
  non-substantial changes.

BACKGROUND

City Park Maintenance staff oversees more than 500 acres of developed parkland,
including 16 ball fields and 27 multi-use fields that support year-round community
programming.

To better align maintenance levels with the park system’s high field use, staff developed
a five-year rest and renovation program guided by the City’s Sports Turf Assessment
and the Parks and Recreation Master Plan. The program addresses turf renovation
needs, coordinates field closures to reduce stakeholder impacts, and ensures adequate
time for turf establishment.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Approve Agrmt No. A-9790 with Greenfield Landscaping and Maintenance, Inc.
April 7, 2026
Page 2

As part of this program, the Marie Kerr Park south soccer field was selected for turf
removal and replacement due to its condition and high demand for community activities.
The field was last renovated in June 2024 using hydroseeding; however, contractor
delays led to excessive weed growth and shortened the establishment window for warm-
season turf. Subsequent winter redirected runoff into the co-located drainage basin,
further affecting soil fertility and turfgrass density.

DISCUSSION

The City released Invitation for Bid (IFB) No. 26-002-3500 for Turf Removal and
Replacement Services on January 20, 2026. The IFB was posted on PlanetBids,
published in the Antelope Valley Press, and listed on the City’s website. A total of 35
prospective bidders viewed the solicitation, and five (5) vendors submitted bids by the
February 24, 2026, deadline.

 Vendor  Location  Bid Amount
 BSI Sports Turf, Inc.  Compton, CA  $114,171.29
 Greenfield Landscaping & Maintenance  Hacienda Heights, CA  $140,800.00
 Landscape Connection Group  Lancaster, CA  $149,700.00
 SGD Enterprises  Van Nuys, CA  $180,000.00
 Sandco Landscape Contractors  Victorville, CA  $498,650.00

In an Invitation for Bids (IFB), price is the primary evaluation factor, as the process is
designed to secure the lowest cost for clearly defined goods or services. Because
specifications are fully detailed in advance, the contract is awarded to the lowest
responsible and responsive bidder who meets all requirements.

BSI Sports Turf, Inc. did not include the required cost for big roll sod installation in its
proposal, rendering its bid nonresponsive. Greenfield Landscaping and Maintenance, Inc.
was the lowest responsive and responsible bid among the qualified vendors.

Under this Agreement, Greenfield Landscaping and Maintenance, Inc., will remove and
replace approximately 117,500 square feet of turf at Marie Kerr Park south soccer field.
The renovation will remove existing weed seed banks, correct acidic soil pH and nutrient
imbalances by incorporating sand and soil conditioners, and time installation to optimize
hybrid Bermuda grass establishment. These improvements, implemented in accordance
with best management practices, will address turf deterioration, enhance field safety and
functionality, and improve overall turf health and durability.

Based on the condition of the field, the cost-effectiveness of turf replacement, staff
recommend that the City Council approve the agreement with Greenfield Landscaping
and Maintenance, Inc.

This project falls under the Community Workforce Agreement.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve Change Order No. 3 & 4 to Agreement No. A-9273 with Deark E&C to
  increase the contract amount by $29,860 for a total contract amount not to
  exceed $590,854 for PN 887, Marie Kerr Park Best of the West Softball
  Complex Concession Stand Project;

BACKGROUND

Project No. 887 involved the construction of a new concession stand for snack and
beverage sales. The scope of work included site preparation, ADA-compliant
improvements, landscaping, and all required utility connections. The City purchased
the ROMTEC concession stand building, and the contractor was responsible for its
construction in accordance with ROMTEC plans and specifications, as well as the
associated ADA upgrades. Additionally, the contractor installed fencing and a single
gate for the outdoor BBQ area at Parks and Recreation's request.

DISCUSSION

On July 1, 2025, the City Council approved the construction agreement with Deark
E&C, Inc. for PN 887, Marie Kerr Park Best of the West Softball Complex Concession
Stand Project (Project), for a not to exceed amount of $560,995, which includes a 10%
contingency for a term of 45 working days. The Project began on August 4, 2025, and
due to the Contract Change Orders listed below, the project was completed on
February 26, 2026, for a total of 85 working days.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: PN 887 Marie Kerr Park Best of the West Concession Stand Project
April 7, 2026
Page 2

Contract Change Order No. 3 was issued to the contractor in response to the Los
Angeles County Health Department’s requirement for a minimum 20-gallon
commercial hot water heater, replacing the instantaneous water heater originally
specified in the contract. Compliance with this requirement necessitated an electrical
panel upgrade to meet the increased electrical demand. The total cost associated
with this change order is $56,166.

Contract Change Order No. 4 was issued following additional requirements from the
Los Angeles County Health Department, which mandated stainless steel cove base,
fiberglass-reinforced plastic wall panels, and drywall wrapping of exposed ceiling
wood beams. The originally approved drawings from the County allowed for tile base
coving, masonry walls, and exposed wood rafters. Due to these last-minute changes
in required materials and finishes, the contract amount increased by an additional
$24,693.

Both contract change orders were necessary to obtain the Los Angeles County Health
Department’s final inspection approval and operational clearance. The total change
order amount exceeds the authorized 10% contingency by 4.8%. Therefore, staff is
requesting an additional $29,860 for the additional work performed.

FISCAL IMPACT

$29,860; Funds are budgeted and available in FY 2026-27 for Change Order No. 3 &
4.

SUBJECT:  ACCEPT NOTICE OF COMPLETION (NOC) FOR PN 918, 2025
  SUMMER ARTERIAL OVERLAY PROJECT

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Accept the NOC for PN 918, 2025 Summer Arterial Overlay Project; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager or his designee to file the NOC and release the
  security for the completed public street improvements.

BACKGROUND

Project No. 918 provided 1,080,430 square feet of asphalt overlay in three separate
districts, see Location Map. The arterial roadways include Avenue R-8, 30th Street
East, and Avenue O. This project expanded bicycle routes and connectivity for the
neighborhoods served by the Tumbleweed Dual Immersion School. Continuing with
the improvements along Avenue R-8 from 27th to 35th Street East, this project
increased safety and walkability to the Cactus Magnet Academy. The striping
improvements included bike lanes, 6-inch lane lines in highly reflective thermoplastic
material, and the upgrading of existing crosswalks to the new continental style along
the arterial cross streets, increasing both visibility and safety for Palmdale residents.

On September 2, 2025, the City Council approved the award of a construction
agreement with Hardy & Harper, Inc. for Project No. 918, for an amount not to exceed
$4,163,500, which included a contract amount of $3,785,000 and a 10% contingency
in the amount of $378,500. A notice to proceed with construction was issued on
October 6, 2025. The completion date was established as January 6, 2026, including
the original contract term, weather\non-working days, and additional workdays
authorized during construction. The project was field accepted as complete prior to that
date; however, a large storm event in early January 2026 caused substantial damage
to a section of roadway on Avenue O at the Big Rock Wash crossing. Staff coordinated
 Report to Mayor and City Council

with the Contractor to repair the damage, which involved removing and replacing the
roadway and securing an exposed gas main, as an extra to the project, to be completed
by January 30, 2026. Contractor expedited the repair, and Avenue O was reopened to
traffic on January 16, 2026, whereupon all project work was accepted as complete.

DISCUSSION

Construction of the project was completed on time and within budget, reflecting
change orders and additional time authorized and approved by staff. Approved
change orders included resurfacing the asphalt-concrete berm on 30th St East,
signing and striping of bike lanes on Avenue R-8, and the storm damage repair on
Avenue O. The total of the approved change orders amounted to $298,473.74, which
is within the 10% contingency.

FISCAL IMPACT

$0; There is no fiscal impact associated with this action. Project costs, including
construction, contract observation, material testing, labor compliance, and various
administrative costs, totaled $4,019,479.18 and were funded entirely using Gas Tax
(S0025201).

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Nominate and appoint one public member to the Palmdale EIFD PFA to serve the
  remainder of a two-year term set to expire June 30, 2027.

BACKGROUND

The Palmdale EIFD and PFA were established on June 1, 2021, by Resolution No. CC
2021-044. The primary goal of the Palmdale EIFD is to implement the Palmdale
Enhanced Infrastructure Financing Plan to attract new private sector investment,
accelerate development in key areas of the City, stimulate job creation, expand housing
opportunities, and strengthen local and regional transportation options for the region.

The PFA is a separate body that oversees the Palmdale EIFD. The PFA includes two
members of the City Council, a public member selected by the Council, one County
member, and a public member selected by the County.

Meetings are held on a as needed basis in the Council Chamber, 38300 Sierra
Highway, Suite B, Palmdale, CA.

DISCUSSION

Board Member Gordon resigned on January 15, 2026, creating a vacancy. Due to the
resignation, this action allows the City Council to nominate and appoint one public
member to fill the vacancy.

  Assistant classification; and, further, recognizing Teamsters Union Local 986 as
  the exclusive representative for the newly formed unit.

BACKGROUND

The City of Palmdale is subject to the Meyers-Milias-Brown Act (MMBA), which provides
employees with the right to representation regarding wages, hours, and other terms and
conditions of employment. In accordance with these provisions, the City received a
formal request from the California Teamsters, Local 986, (“Teamsters”) to include
employees in the Public Works Maintenance Division employed in the classifications of
Superintendent, Analyst, Administrative Assistant, and Office Assistant in the existing
bargaining unit composed of those Department of Public Works Maintenance Division
classifications identified in Section 1.02 of the current Memorandum of Understanding
(“MOU” between the Teamsters and the City). In the alternative, the Teamsters
proposed creating a separate unit of these proposed classifications. The Teamsters’
request was accompanied by ‘representation petitions’ signed and dated by the
employee incumbents in the proposed classifications, authorizing the Teamsters to
serve as their ‘sole and exclusive representative for collective bargaining’. The
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Adopt Reso. No. CC 2026-017
April 7, 2026
Page 2

Teamsters also requested that the City’s Human Resources (HR) Department review
the job classifications and criteria for determining unit classifications.

Upon receiving this request, staff conducted an evaluation of the classifications listed,
Superintendent, Analyst, Administrative Assistant, and Office Assistant, to determine
whether they share a sufficient community of interest in accordance with the MMBA, for
inclusion in the current bargaining unit. The review considered job duties, organizational
structure, working conditions, and supervisory responsibilities.

DISCUSSION

Based on the job analysis assessment, HR staff determined that the Superintendent,
Analyst, and Administrative Assistant classifications are aligned in their supervisory and
administrative functions within the Maintenance Division of the Public Works
Department. Their duties and organizational roles demonstrated a shared community of
interest that was more appropriate for establishing a separate bargaining unit for the
Public Works Maintenance Division Supervisory and Confidential staff classifications,
rather than for inclusion in the existing Teamsters bargaining unit.

The review also found that the Office Assistant classification differs substantially in job
function and organizational alignment. The Office Assistant classification performs
clerical and administrative functions that do not align with the supervisory and
operational duties. Additionally, this role does not involve access to confidential
information, further supporting exclusion from this new unit. For this reason, it is more
appropriately placed within the existing Public Works Maintenance Division employee
bargaining unit rather than in the proposed new unit.

As required under the applicable provisions of the MMBA, City representatives met with
the Teamsters bargaining unit representatives on four (4) occasions regarding the
Union’s requests to modify the existing bargaining unit or create a separate bargaining
unit. The City and the Teamsters have agreed to the creation of a new bargaining unit
to be represented by Teamsters, Local 986.

Establishing the Public Works Maintenance Division Supervisory and Confidential Unit
will help clarify supervisory structures and support effective labor relations. Recognizing
Teamsters Union Local 986 as their exclusive representative will allow these employees
to engage in collective bargaining that reflects the unique needs of the Maintenance
Division’s supervisory and administrative staff.

FISCAL IMPACT

$0; There is no immediate fiscal impact associated with establishing the bargaining unit
or recognizing the exclusive representative. Future negotiations under a Memorandum

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Receive public testimony regarding proposed Ordinance No. 1667; and,

  2. Adopt Ordinance No. 1667 approving Zoning Ordinance Amendment (ZOA)
  26-0002; and,

  3. Find that the request is exempt from environmental review.

BACKGROUND

In 2025, the State of California enacted and amended Government Code Sections
66310 through 66342 to facilitate the development of ADUs and JADUs. These statutes
preempt local regulations that conflict with State law. The City’s current ADU and JADU
regulations were adopted prior to these amendments and the renumbering of the State
ADU law. A review of the Palmdale Municipal Code (PMC) identified provisions that are
no longer consistent with State requirements and must be updated to ensure
compliance.

On March 19, 2026, the Planning Commission adopted Resolution No. PC-2026-003
recommending City Council approval of ZOA 26-0002.
 Report to Mayor and City Council

April 7, 2026
Page 2

DISCUSSION

In recent years, the California Legislature has enacted laws to address the State’s
housing shortage by facilitating the development of ADUs and JADUs. These laws limit
local regulation of ADUs and JADUs and require local ordinances to be consistent with
State law.

The proposed amendments update PMC Chapter 17.91.010 (Accessory dwelling unit
and junior accessory dwelling unit standards) to ensure compliance with Government
Code Sections 66310 through 66342. Updates include revising statutory citations,
clarifying ministerial review of ADU applications, updating provisions related to the
number and size of ADUs and JADUs, revising deed restriction and owner-occupancy
provisions, and clarifying that construction of an ADU does not trigger a requirement to
install fire sprinklers in an existing primary dwelling.

ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW

The proposed ZOA is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
pursuant to Public Resource Code Section 21080.17, which exempts the adoption of
an ordinance implementing the provisions of State law relating to ADUs and JADUs.

FISCAL IMPACT

$0; There is no proposed development; therefore, this action has no fiscal impact;
however, it will facilitate the development of different housing types, which will increase
property value.
